title: Life in the palace
hookLine: music, gardens, the king's fear that his son will leave (Buddhacarita 2)

cards: In the evenings, music drifts down from the upper rooms of the palace. Women play and sing. The rooms open onto gardens.
Down below, the poem says, the whole land seems to flourish after the boy is born. Everything a young prince could want is brought upstairs to him. And the man who arranged all of it is afraid.
It's the king. He keeps hearing an old sage's voice telling him his son will leave the kingdom. So he has decided what to do about it.

teach.h: THE PALACE, SEEN THROUGH THE FATHER.
teach.b: Year one told the palace years from the prince's side, in his own later words: three palaces, one for each season, and a life of great comfort. The poem moves the camera. It shows the palace through his father.

First, the plan. The poem says plainly why the king fills the prince's days with pleasure: he remembers what Asita foretold, and wants the boy so delighted with home that he never thinks of the forest.
The music isn't only a gift. It's a strategy. Second, the details.

The prince grows up in the upper rooms, among music and dancing, while out in the kingdom the king rules well and does good works, as if he could hold everything steady by being good enough. Third, the family.
The king arranges a marriage, to Yashodhara, and in time a son is born, Rahula.

teach.h: A WIFE, A SON, ONE MORE THREAD.
teach.b: The king is glad: a grandson is one more thread holding the prince to home. And fourth, the fear underneath. Nothing in the palace is cruel.

teach.h: EVERY GIFT IS ALSO A WALL.
teach.b: Every gift is real, and every gift is also a wall. The king isn't a villain; he's a father trying to write his son's story for him.
Some listeners will know that father. Some have been him. The poem doesn't mock him.
It shows how hard he's holding on, and quietly suggests the holding won't be enough.

how: Buddhist teachers draw on the palace years when speaking about comfort, attachment and family love, and the story appears in temple murals and in children's classes in Buddhist communities.

games.q: what does “life in the palace” mean?
o: comfort arranged to keep the prince from leaving
a lavish life the prince chose for himself
the king's training of his son to rule

games.q: the palace in the poem: tap the pairs.
p: keep him too happy to leave

s: in the poem, the king fills the palace with pleasure by accident
the poem says he does it on purpose, remembering Asita's words.
the poem paints the king as a cruel jailer
every gift is real; he is a loving father who is afraid.
year one told the palace from the prince's side
in his own later words: three palaces and a life of comfort. the poem shows the father's side.

games.q: you're the king. a sage has said your son will leave the throne for the forest. what do you do?
o: tell your son the prophecy and let him choose.
fill his life with every pleasure so he never wants to leave.
send him away to train as a monk now.
games.why: the king surrounds him with music, gardens, a marriage. love, and a plan, and a fear.

practice: Look gently around the life you have for one thing you've been protected from: a hard truth a parent kept from you when you were small, trouble your neighborhood keeps out of sight, a phone that shows you only what you already like.
Don't judge whoever built the wall, and don't tear it down in your head; just see it, and notice whether it came from love, or fear, or both.

wordCard.voice: Life in the palace. Music, gardens, a marriage and a son, all arranged by a king who fears his son will leave. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit: a palace or mansion, a raised building with upper floors.

carryVoice: Your line: a father's fear. Tomorrow, something finally gets through the walls. That's day seven hundred.
